recent_posts.title: Why you should leave GitHub and what to use instead
recent_posts.summary: GitHub's reliability and quality have declined significantly under Microsoft's ownership, with increasing downtime, bot spam, AI slop, and a degraded developer experience. The post argues developers should migrate away from GitHub and explores alternatives including Codeberg (Forgejo-based, non-profit), Tangled, Gitea, GitLab, and Bitbucket. Self-hosting Forgejo is recommended as the best option for those willing to manage their own infrastructure. The author emphasizes that Git itself is decentralized and open source — GitHub is just one optional layer on top.

recent_posts.title: On AI, techno-fascism and developers quitting in protest
recent_posts.summary: A critical opinion piece on the AI industrial complex and techno-fascism, arguing that the tech industry's uncritical embrace of AI tools is driven by greed and complicity rather than genuine utility. The author draws on stories of developers quitting in protest, discusses the harm AI mandates are causing to careers and mental health, and calls out the 'it's just a tool' crowd as naive or complicit. The piece ends on a personal note about reclaiming creativity and agency as resistance.

recent_posts.title: Web tools are cool
recent_posts.summary: A personal blog post sharing a curated list of web-based developer tools the author uses regularly. Highlights include Squoosh for image optimization, Can I Use for browser compatibility checks, a CSS specificity calculator, and ReliCSS. The author also reflects on hosting side projects and invites readers to suggest their own favourite web tools.

recent_posts.title: CSS cascade layers and the !important containment breach
recent_posts.summary: CSS cascade layers are supposed to solve specificity wars, but they have surprising edge cases. Using custom property fallback values is an effective escape hatch when a utility layer class needs to be overridden by a component layer. More surprisingly, !important declarations in lower cascade layers actually breach containment and override higher layers — with the lowest layer's !important winning — which feels counterintuitive and causes real problems in messy ecosystems like WordPress where plugins rely on !important.

recent_posts.title: No-stack web development
recent_posts.summary: A developer argues against adopting a default web development stack, outlining four core problems: technical debt from prescribing solutions before diagnosing problems, non-transferable knowledge that abstracts away from web fundamentals, accelerated obsolescence from churnware with breaking changes, and vendor lock-in that sacrifices long-term stability. The recommendation is to default to CSS, HTML, and JavaScript as the true web stack, choosing additional tools only when their impact is understood and they align with project goals rather than developer preferences. React is singled out as a legacy framework to avoid.

recent_posts.title: How CSS subgrid simplifies complex CMS layout patterns
recent_posts.summary: CSS subgrid makes complex CMS-driven layouts much easier to implement. Using a named-line grid on a `<main>` element, child elements can break out to full viewport width or a boxed margin style with a single class, then re-align their inner content back to the readable column using `grid-template-columns: subgrid`. The technique avoids negative margins and repetitive wrapper divs, and works well with WordPress block editor or ACF flexible content output. A CodePen demo shows a two-column variant where text edges align while an image covers the full available space.

recent_posts.title: Common Figma design decisions that cause problems in responsive web development
recent_posts.summary: A web developer's critique of common Figma design pitfalls that create problems during implementation. Covers issues like full-width banners with unclear responsive behavior, focal point ambiguity across breakpoints, arbitrary line breaks that don't translate to real web rendering, and the proliferation of breakpoints. The core argument is that these 'betrayals' stem from Figma's inability to represent the fluid, responsive nature of the web, and that the real solution is early collaboration between designers, developers, and content authors — not more design iterations in isolation.

recent_posts.title: A front-end developer starts a hobby game development project
recent_posts.summary: A front-end developer reflects on their roots in Flash/ActionScript and shares a personal goal to explore game development as a hobby. They've built small HTML canvas prototypes and plan to dedicate a few hours weekly to game-related creative work, inspired partly by playing Slay the Spire 2. The project is framed as a deliberate, AI-free creative retreat.

recent_posts.title: RSS Club #006: Burnout
recent_posts.summary: A personal, RSS-only post from a freelance web developer reflecting on possible burnout. The author discusses physical setbacks from a hamstring injury, growing frustration with the tech and web industry's direction, the tension between writing opinionated content versus evergreen helpful posts, and uncertainty about whether venting online is productive or a symptom of burnout itself.

recent_posts.title: SMTP on the edge
recent_posts.summary: A developer replaces their Cloudflare Worker + AWS SES contact form setup with a new approach: PGP encryption in the browser, a POST to a Bunny edge worker (Deno-based), and direct SMTP to Proton Mail. After discovering that raw SMTP from Bunny edge scripts is technically possible but discouraged by Bunny support, the final solution forwards encrypted data from the Bunny worker to a self-hosted API that handles SMTP. This eliminates AWS and Cloudflare as intermediaries, achieving true end-to-end encryption for the contact form.
